title: Old-Time Beet & Turnip Storage
subtitle: Tips From a 1917 USDA Bulletin
desc: Old-time beet and turnip storage tips from USDA Farmers' Bulletin 879, Home Storage of Vegetables (1917), checked against today's advice: harvest before a hard freeze, trim tops to half an inch, brush off soil without washing, and layer in damp sand in a cold, humid root cellar near 32–40°F. Strong-smelling turnips do best in an outdoor pit or garage.

title: How to Pressure Can Potatoes
subtitle: USDA Tested Method
desc: How to can potatoes safely in a pressure canner, following the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning: peel and cube, boil 2 minutes, hot pack with fresh boiling water and 1-inch headspace, then process pints 35 minutes and quarts 40 at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–1,000 ft) or 11 lb (dial gauge); adjust for altitude. Never can mashed potatoes or water bath potatoes.

title: Freeze Apple Slices for Pie
subtitle: Bake Fresh Pies All Winter
desc: How to freeze apple slices for pies: peel, core and slice, dip in an ascorbic acid (vitamin C) solution to stop browning, tray freeze in a single layer, then bag with the air pressed out. Best quality within 8–12 months, so you can bake homemade apple pie all winter.

title: Cook Safely in a Power Outage
subtitle: Avoid Carbon Monoxide
desc: How to cook safely during a winter power outage: never use a grill, camp stove or generator indoors or in a garage, keep generators at least 20 feet from windows and doors, run a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm, and stock no-cook pantry foods plus a manual can opener. Emergency preparedness for the self-sufficient home.

title: Use Fall Leaves in the Garden
subtitle: Free Mulch and Compost
items: Pile wet leaves for leaf mold
desc: How to use fall leaves in the vegetable garden: shred them with a mower, spread 2–3 inches as winter mulch on empty beds, pile wet leaves to make leaf mold, or mix them into compost. Avoid black walnut leaves. A free way to build better garden soil for spring.
